q: Atoms consist of three sub-atomic particles called proton, neutron and electron.
e: These three particles are the fundamental particles that make up an atom.

q: Proton, neutron and electron are also known as compound particles.
e: Proton, neutron and electron are known as fundamental particles, not compound particles.

q: A proton is a particle carrying a negative charge.
e: A proton is a particle carrying a positive charge.

q: A neutron is a particle carrying no charge and having a mass similar to proton.
e: Neutrons are neutral and their mass is approximately equal to that of a proton.

q: The mass of an electron is approximately 1/1837 times the mass of a proton.
e: Electrons have a very small mass compared to protons and neutrons.

q: The relative mass of an electron is 1.
e: The relative mass of an electron is 1/1837, while the relative mass of a proton and neutron is 1.

q: In a neutral atom, the number of protons is equal to the number of electrons.
e: The positive charges of protons balance the negative charges of electrons in a neutral atom.

q: Atoms are identified by the number of neutrons in it.
e: Atoms are identified by the number of protons in it, which is the atomic number.

q: The proton number is often referred to as the atomic number (Z) of the element.
e: The atomic number (Z) represents the number of protons in an atom's nucleus.

q: Different elements have the same proton number or atomic number from each other.
e: Different elements have a different proton number or atomic number from each other.

q: The atom has a small, dense, positively charged center called nucleus.
e: The nucleus contains the positively charged protons and neutral neutrons.

q: The nucleus contains proton(s) and electron(s).
e: The nucleus contains proton(s) and neutron(s), while electrons are found outside the nucleus.

q: The total number of protons and neutrons is also known as the nucleon number or mass number (A).
e: Mass number (A) is the sum of the number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.

q: Outside and around the nucleus, electrons rapidly move in circular or near circular orbits.
e: Electrons occupy the space surrounding the nucleus in specific energy levels or orbits.

q: Isotopes are atoms with the same number of protons but different number of neutrons.
e: Isotopes of an element share the same atomic number but have different mass numbers.

q: Isotopes are the atoms of different elements with different masses.
e: Isotopes are the atoms of the same element with different masses.

q: All atoms of the same element have the same number of protons.
e: The number of protons defines the element, so it remains constant for all atoms of that element.

q: Most of carbon atoms have 6 neutrons but some carbon atoms are found with 7 neutrons or 8 neutrons.
e: These variations in neutron number create the isotopes Carbon-12, Carbon-13, and Carbon-14.

q: Carbon-14 is a stable atom.
e: Carbon-14 is an unstable, radioactive atom, whereas Carbon-12 and Carbon-13 are stable.

q: Mass spectrometer is a device used to find out the masses of isotopes and their relative abundance.
e: It is also used as a means of measuring the ionisation energy of all elements.

q: Isotopes of the same element have different chemical properties but the same physical properties.
e: Isotopes of the same element have the same chemical properties but there are some small differences in physical properties.

q: A carbon-14 atom is radioactive but carbon-12 and carbon-13 are not radioactive.
e: Carbon-14 produces radiation, while the other two common carbon isotopes do not.

q: Most isotopes in the air and ground are radioactive.
e: Most isotopes in the air and ground are not radioactive.

q: Isobars are different elements with different proton number and same nucleon number.
e: Isobars have the same mass number (A) but different atomic numbers (Z).

q: Up to the early 20th century, uranium was used in making an attractive yellow glaze for pottery.
e: This practice ended when people realised that uranium is radioactive, making the pots radioactive too.

q: Cobalt-60 (Co-60) is used in radiotherapy and in food preservation.
e: Co-60 is a radioisotope with beneficial applications in medicine and industry.

q: P-32 and Sr-90 are used to treat skin cancer.
e: These radioactive isotopes are applied in the treatment of hazardous diseases like skin cancer.

q: Na-24 is used to detect tumors and blood clots and also detect the leakage from underground pipes.
e: Na-24 is a useful radioisotope for both medical diagnostics and industrial leak detection.

q: I-131 is used to investigate the thyroid glands.
e: Iodine-131 is specifically utilized in medical investigations of thyroid function.

q: C-14 is widely used in estimation of the age of ancient artifacts by radiocarbon dating method.
e: The predictable decay of radioactive Carbon-14 allows scientists to date organic materials.

q: Atoms are the smallest particles into which an element can be divided.
e: This is a fundamental definition of an atom in chemistry.

q: The atomic number changes depending on the chemical reaction.
e: The atomic number never changes; it is a fixed property of the element.
